claims.text: In situ heating transmission electron microscopy can reveal atomic-scale rearrangements in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles as temperature increases.
In situ heating TEM can reveal temperature-induced phase transitions in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The initial nanoparticles have a homogeneous, random atomic distribution at room temperature.
Atomic-resolution imaging during incremental heating can track changes in nanoparticle structure.
A high-vacuum or inert environment minimizes oxidation during in situ heating.
Controlled heating rates help minimize imaging drift and permit atomic-scale resolution at successive temperature steps.
Thermal activation may change atomic lattice organization and interatomic distances.
Thermal activation may induce local chemical segregation or ordering.
Increasing thermal energy activates atomic diffusion and rearrangement in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermally activated diffusion and rearrangement may cause segregation, lattice-parameter changes, or phase transitions.
Exceeding a critical temperature will produce observable changes in atomic positions, lattice distortions, segregation, ordering, or distinct phases relative to the room-temperature configuration.
The detectable results are constrained by the spatial resolution and operating-temperature range of the in situ TEM.
Nanoparticle size and local composition fluctuations may affect the temperature threshold and degree of atomic rearrangement.
